title: Which numbers should you know by heart for market sizing?
description: Rough population, household and time figures that make market sizing faster, plus how to use them and what to do when you do not know a number.
hook: You need about a dozen round numbers by heart: the populations of the world, the big countries and a few cities, household counts and sizes for the UK and US, and the basic time units (days, weeks, working days and working hours in a year). Everything else in a market sizing question you can derive from those or state as an assumption. Interviewers care about your logic, not your memory, but these anchors let you start quickly and spot an answer that is out by a factor of ten.
body:
People

Rounded the way you would use them in a case, with the latest figure behind each one:

PlaceRound numberLatest estimate
World8 billionNearly 8.2B in mid-2024 (UN)
India and China1.4 billion eachIndia now slightly ahead
European Union450 millionAbout 450M on 1 January 2025 (Eurostat)
United States340 million341.8M in July 2025 (Census Bureau)
Germany / France84M / 68MFrance including overseas departments
United Kingdom68 to 70 million69.5M provisional, mid-2025 (ONS)
London / New York City9M / 8.5MLondon 9.1M in mid-2024 (ONS)

Our worked examples use 68M for the UK because it divides neatly; 70M is just as acceptable. What matters is that you say the number and why you chose it.

Households

  • UK: about 28M households (the ONS counted 28.6M in 2024), at about 2.4 people each.
  • US: about 135M households (the Census Bureau's 2025 survey put it at 134.8M), at about 2.5 people each.

You can rebuild either from the population: 69.5M ÷ 2.4 is about 29M; 340M ÷ 2.5 is about 136M. Use households whenever the thing you are sizing is bought or used by a home: parcels, broadband, washing machines, pizza deliveries, pianos.

Work

  • UK: about 30M employees on payrolls (HMRC data, 2026), plus around 4M self-employed.
  • US: about 163M people in work (Bureau of Labor Statistics household survey, August 2026).

These help with business-to-business questions such as office chairs bought by UK employers, where you start from desk workers rather than from everyone.

Time

  • A year: 365 days, 52 weeks, about 8,760 hours.
  • Working days: about 220 to 250 a year, depending on holidays and leave.
  • Working hours for one full-time person: about 1,800 to 2,000 a year.
  • Life expectancy in rich countries: about 80 years. Population ÷ 80 gives a rough number of people at each year of age.

The last one is surprisingly useful. The UK has about 69.5M ÷ 80 = roughly 870,000 people per year of age, so about 870,000 ten-year-olds or 17-year-olds learning to drive. The US has about 340M ÷ 80 = 4.25M. It is rough (age groups are not equal in size), but it gets you the right order of magnitude in one step.

Derive, don't memorise

You do not need a large stock of statistics. With the anchors above, you can build almost anything:

  • Households from population ÷ household size.
  • People in an age band from population ÷ 80 × number of years in the band.
  • Capacity from working days × hours × output per hour, as in how many dentists the UK needs.
  • Daily figures from yearly figures ÷ 365, or weekly ÷ 7.

When a result looks surprising, re-check the units before you change an assumption. Most big errors are unit errors, not bad guesses.

When you do not know a number

Say so, and make a sensible assumption out loud, or ask:

"I don't know the exact number of UK households, so I'll assume about 28 million, from roughly 68 million people at 2.4 per home."
"Do we have a figure for the number of vehicles, or shall I estimate it?"

Both are fine. What is not fine is freezing, or stating a precise number such as "28.63 million" with no explanation. False precision suggests you are bluffing.

Round, and say you are rounding

Choose numbers that make the maths easy: 68M becomes 70M, 52 weeks becomes 50, 365 days becomes 360 if you are dividing by 12. Say "I'll round to 70 million to keep the maths simple". At the end, check whether your roundings all pushed the answer the same way; if they did, adjust. For multiplying large numbers cleanly, see how to multiply big numbers without losing the zeros.

Common mistakes with anchor numbers

  • People where you need households. In a country of 60M people at 2.5 per home there are 24M households. Use people by mistake and your answer is 2.5 times too big.
  • Population where you need workers. The UK has about 69.5M people but only around 34M in work.
  • Quoting old figures as current. A population from 2024 is fine as a round anchor in 2026, but present it as an approximation, not a precise current statistic.
  • Mixing geographies. London, Greater London and the London commuter belt are different numbers. So are the city of Paris and Greater Paris.

Practise it

1. Roughly how many UK children start primary school each year?

Show the answer

One year group: about 69.5M ÷ 80 = roughly 870,000. Recent birth cohorts are smaller than the average year of age, so the true figure is noticeably lower, but the method gets you to the right scale instantly.

2. How many households are there in London?

Show the answer

9M people ÷ about 2.5 per household = about 3.6M households. London homes tend to be slightly larger than the UK average of 2.4, so 2.5 is a reasonable choice; say why you picked it.

3. How many hours do UK employees work in total in a year?

Show the answer

30M employees × 1,800 hours = about 54B hours. Many work part time, so the full-time 1,800 figure overstates it; a candidate who says so earns credit.
